<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-landmine-policy","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540372"} -->
## Creating a Landmine Policy

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-landmine-policy
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Landmine Decoys > Policies > Creating a Landmine Policy
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to create a landmine policy in the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal.

[Watch a video on Creating Landmine Policies and Decoys.](https://fast.wistia.net/embed/iframe/c3w5mose6l)

Landmine decoys are configured based on policies. Policies consist of various options, such as decoy files, processes, lures, etc. that can be applied to an endpoint. Each policy has a selection criterion, and the policy is applied to the endpoint only if the criterion matches.

Before creating landmine policies, obtain information about the list of users, hostnames, and selection criteria.

To create a landmine policy:

- Step 1: Add a Landmine Policy
- Step 2: Specify a Selection Criterion
- Step 3: Configure the Lure Modules in the Landmine Policy

1. Go to **Deceive** > **Landmine**> **Policies**.
2. Click **Add Policy**. See image. The **Policy Details** window appears.
3. In the **Policy Details** window: See image.
  1. **Enabled**: Select to enable the policy.
  2. **Policy Name**: Enter a name for the policy. The name can be a user or system persona. For example, enter `IT Admins`.
  3. **OS**: Select an operating system of endpoints to which the policy should apply.
  4. **Agentless**: Enable to deploy the policy in the agentless mode. By default, a policy is deployed in the agent mode. The agentless policy applies only to the agentless version of Landmine, and the agent policy applies only to the agent version of Landmine.
4. Click **Save**. The policy is added. See image.

After the landmine policy is added, you need to specify a selection criterion. The landmine agent fetches the policy from the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal and applies it to the endpoints based on the selection criterion. If you are unsure about the criterion, specify the Catch All criterion to apply the policy to all of the landmine agents.

To specify a selection criterion:

1. On the **Policies** tab, locate the landmine policy, and then click the **Edit** icon. See image.
2. In the policy configuration window, click **Selection Criterion**. See image.
3. In the **Selection Criterion** window, choose a criterion from the drop-down menu:
  - **Catch All**: Apply the policy to all landmine agents. See image.
  - **Dynamic Rule**: Choose an option from the **Attribute** drop-down menu: Click **Add** to add multiple dynamic rules to a single policy. If *any one* of the rules matches, the policy is applied at the endpoint. See image.
    - **Process List**: Apply the policy to the endpoints that contain the processes specified in the **Contains** field. This is a substring of the process executable (e.g., `chrome`, `cmd`, and `winword.exe`).
    - **Browser History**: Apply the policy to the endpoints whose browser history has the URL specified in the **Contains** field. This is a substring of URLs (e.g., `192.168.89.23`, `google.com`, and `https://www.zscaler.com`).
    - **Installed Programs**: Apply the policy to the endpoints that contain the installed programs specified in the **Contains** field. This is a substring of the names of applications (e.g., `Google Chrome`, `Microsoft Office`, and `Firefox`).
    - **Interesting Files**: Apply the policy to the endpoints that contain the files specified in the **Contains** field. This is a substring of the names of files (e.g., `passwords.txt`, `finance details`, and `ID Document`).
    - **Recent Commands**: Apply the policy to the endpoints whose recent command list in the **Run** dialog box matches the commands specified in the **Contains** field (e.g., the list of comments that have been run from the Run prompt on Windows).
  - **User**: Apply the policy to all the endpoints where at least one of the users specified in the **User** field is logged in. You can enter the usernames in the **User** field, or click **Upload** to upload a text file with the usernames. To apply policies to Zscaler Client Connector users, specify their Zscaler Client Connector username. You can also export the list of users as a text file. See image.
  - **Group**: Apply the policy to all the endpoints that are under the Active Directory (AD) groups specified in the **Group** field. You can enter the group names in the **Group** field, or click **Upload** to upload a text file with the group names. You can export the list of group names as a text file. Only AD security groups are supported.; Policies are applied to agents within a maximum of one day.; IdP groups are not supported. See image.
  - **Hostname (Specific)**: Apply the policy to all the endpoints where the hostname of the system exactly matches one of the hostnames specified in the **Hostname** field. You can enter the hostnames in the **Hostname** field, or click **Upload** to upload a text file with the hostnames. You can export the list of hostnames as a text file. See image.
  - **Hostname (RegEx)**: Apply the policy to all landmine agents where the hostname of the system matches the hostname pattern specified as a regular expression in the **RegEx** field. See image.
  - **DNS Hostname (Specific)**: Apply the policy to all endpoints whose FQDN matches with one of the FQDN values specified in the **Hostname**field. You can enter the hostnames in the **Hostname** field, or click **Upload** to upload a text file with the hostnames. You can export the list of hostnames as a text file. See image.
  - **DNS Hostname (RegEx)**: Apply the policy to all landmine agents where the FQDN of the system matches the FQDN pattern specified as a regular expression in the **RegEx** field. See image.
  - **User OU (RegEx)**: Apply the policy to all the users present in the organization unit (OU) that matches the OU regular expression pattern in the **RegEx** field. Policies are applied to agents within a maximum of one day. See image.
  - **Computer OU (RegEx)**: Apply the policy to all the systems present in the OU that match the OU regular expression pattern in the **RegEx** field. Policies are applied to agents within a maximum of one day. See image.
  - **Fallback**: Apply the policy to any system that has no other policy criteria specified. If you have specified the **Catch All**criterion, then the **Fallback** criterion is not applied. See image.
4. Click **Save**. The specified selection criterion is listed in the **Policies** table. See image.

After the selection criterion is specified, you can configure the required lure modules:

- [Password Settings](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/customizing-lure-passwords)
- [Defense Evasion](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-defense-evasion)
- [Privilege Escalation](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-privilege-escalation)
- [Cloud Lures](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-cloud-lures)
- [Browser Lures](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-browser-lures)
- [Session Lures](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-session-lures)
- [File Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-file-decoys)
- [Lure Settings](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/customizing-lure-settings)
- [Advanced Deception Capabilities](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-advanced-deception-capabilities)

## Creating a Managed Identity Decoy in Azure

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-managed-identity-decoy-azure
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > Azure > Creating a Managed Identity Decoy in Azure
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure a managed identity decoy in Microsoft Azure.

Managed identities provide an automatically managed identity in Azure AD (Entra ID) for applications to use when connecting to resources that support Azure AD (Entra ID) authentication. You can create a managed identity decoy (user-defined) that has access to all other decoy resources in a decoy resource group (Decoys Resource Group) [configured by Zscaler Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure). This managed identity decoy can be attached to your production resources. It can also be included in your deployment templates to add deception capabilities to your production resources. If an adversary compromises any of the production resources, they will be lured toward the decoys.

To learn about the list of Azure services that can be attached to managed identities, refer to the [Microsoft Technical Documentation](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/managed-identities-status%23services-supporting-managed-identities&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1690783640140469&usg=AOvVaw23RfBJmYz2ZT5ILux1DJoh).

Deception does not associate the managed identity with any production resources.

## Prerequisites

Before creating a managed identity decoy in Azure, you must ensure that you have:

- Configured the [integration between Microsoft Azure and Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure).
- (Optional) Obtained the necessary PowerShell command to run the deployment script using one of the following methods: This only applies to the Cloud Shell-based deployment.
  - [Automated Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script)
  - [Manual Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script)

## Creating a Managed Identity Decoy

To create a managed identity decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **Azure**> **Managed Identity**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The**Managed Identity Decoy** window appears.
3. In the**Managed Identity Decoy** window: See image.
  - **Name**: Enter a name for the managed identity decoy.
  - **Tenant ID**: Select the tenant ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Subscription ID**: Select the subscription ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Resource Group**: If this is your first decoy in the account (Tenant ID and Subscription ID combination) or if you want to create a new resource group, enter a name for the resource group that must hold the decoy. If there is an existing resource group for the account (Tenant ID and Subscription ID combination), select the resource group from the drop-down menu.
  - **Region**: Select the region where the decoy must be deployed from the drop-down menu. If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.
  - **Description**: Enter a description relevant to the managed identity decoy.
4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoy based on the method used to configure the integration between Azure and Deception: If you want to add multiple managed identity decoys to Microsoft Azure, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then run the script to sync all decoys simultaneously.
  - Terraform-based deployment
  - Cloud Shell-based deployment

Upon successful deployment, the managed identity decoy is added to Microsoft Azure under the Decoys Resource Group configured by Deception [during the integration](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure). The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the managed identity decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > Azure > Managed Identity) within the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. To learn how to configure lures using managed identity decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using Azure Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-azure-decoys).

1. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**.
2. Locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
3. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
4. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
5. Locate the `backend` block in the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of an Azure blob storage-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "azurerm": { "resource_group_name": "your-tfstate-rg", "storage_account_name": "yourtfstatestorageacct", "container_name": "tfstate", "key": "deception/terraform.tfstate" } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same Azure account.
6. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
7. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
8. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted. The necessary resources are deployed.
9. Run the following command to download the details of the state as a JSON file. `terraform output -json decoys_output > deployment-output.json`A JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
10. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**, locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
11. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

1. Sign in to the [Azure Portal](http://https://portal.azure.com) as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.
2. Launch Cloud Shell by clicking the **Cloud Shell** icon on the top navigation bar. See image. The **Cloud Shell** window appears.
3. In the **Cloud Shell** window: See image.
  1. Set your shell environment to PowerShell.
  2. Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the [automated download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script) or [manual download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script).
  3. Enter the option to deploy user decoys and press `Enter`.

## Creating a Network Decoy Group

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-network-decoy-group
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Deceive Settings > Creating a Network Decoy Group
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to create network Decoy groups to logically organize network and threat intelligence decoysin the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal.

[Watch a video on Zero Trust Network Decoys.](https://fast.wistia.net/embed/iframe/jra2iq1bd6)

A network decoy group allows you to logically organize networks and threat intelligence decoys based on function, location, system type, etc. A decoy group categorizes the detected alerts along logical boundaries. You can create a network decoy group based on:

- Business functions, such as HR, Legal, IT, Accounts, etc.
- Geographic regions, such as USA, APAC, EU, etc.
- System types, such as desktops, laptops, servers, etc.

You can create a network group from the Deceive Settings page or when [creating a network decoy](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-internal-network-decoy).

To create a network decoy group:

1. Go to **Deceive** > **Deceive Settings** > **Network Decoy Groups**.
2. Click **Add Decoy Group**.
3. In the **Network Decoy Group Details** window, enter a name for the group and click **Submit**.

[Image: Configure network group details]

The network decoy group is added to the **Network Decoys Group** table.

[Image: Network decoy group added]

Under **Actions**, click the **Edit** icon to edit the network decoy group or the **Delete** icon to delete the network decoy group.
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-orchestration-rule","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540634"} -->
## Creating an Orchestration Rule

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-orchestration-rule
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Orchestrate  > Orchestration Rules > Creating an Orchestration Rule
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: Information on how to create an orchestration rule in Zscaler Deception Admin Portal.

An orchestration rule allows you to automate various actions performed in the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal based on custom conditions created using a purpose-built query language. Using the orchestration rule, you can automate actions that fall broadly under the following categories:

- Workflow: Automate actions performed on events within the [Investigate dashboard](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/viewing-investigate-dashboard), such as marking an event as safe, deleting an event, or adding a tag to the event.
- Notification: Automate sending alert notifications via emails.
- Response: Automate actions taken on an attacker or device using different Security Operation Center (SOC) tools [integrated with Zscaler Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-containment-integration).

A single orchestration rule can include a combination of actions from these categories. For example, you can automate marking an event as safe and sending an email notification to IT administrators using a single orchestration rule. When you add multiple orchestration rules, Deception evaluates the rules for each event starting from the highest priority to find a matching condition and applies the rule action if the condition matches. If the rule condition does not match, the next rule is evaluated. This process continues until all rules are evaluated. When a rule with a matching condition is found, you can choose to evaluate and apply subsequent rules with matching conditions or stop further rule evaluation. To learn more, see [Processing Rules](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/stop-rule-processing).

To create an orchestration rule:

1. Go to **Orchestrate**> **Rules**.
2. Click **Add Rule**. See image. The **Rule Details**window appears.
3. In the **Rule Details**window:
  1. Under the **General**section: See image.
    1. **Name**: Enter a name for the rule.
    2. **Enabled**: Select to enable the rule.
    3. **Don't process further rules**:(Optional) Select to stop the evaluation of subsequent rules if this rule is applied.
    4. **Only ThreatParse Events:** (Optional) Select to apply this rule only for events that have a ThreatParse score.
    5. Create a rule condition using queries. To learn how to build queries, see [Understanding and Building Queries](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/understanding-and-building-queries). If no condition is configured, then the rule is applied to all events.
    6. **Time Zone**: Select a time zone that should be used to evaluate rules if you used date and time fields in the queries in the previous step.
  2. Configure one or more categories of automation:
    - Workflow
    - Notification
    - Response
4. Click **Save**.

You can create a rule to automatically perform workflow actions such as tagging, deleting, or marking security events or alerts as safe.

To do this, under the **Workflow**section, configure one or more workflow actions:

- **Mark as safe**: Enable to mark the events that match the condition as safe.
- **Delete**: Enable to delete the events that match the condition.
- **Add Tags**: Enable and enter a tag name to tag the events that match the condition. For example, if the rule condition is `attacker.ip is "192.0.2.3"` and the tag name is `Team A`, then all events from the IP address 192.0.2.3 are tagged as Team A.

See image.

You can create a rule to automatically send alert notifications about events to specific users via email. The rule generates a notification whenever an event matches the rule conditions.

To do this, under the **Notify**section, configure an email notification:

- Enable **Email**.
- Select the users you want to notify via email from the drop-down menu.
- Select the email notification frequency from the drop-down menu. See image.

- The notifications use default templates and are sent to the email address [configured for the user](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-users-roles#deception-add-new-user-admin-portal). You can also customize the notification template. To learn more, see [Customizing Event Notification Templates](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/customizing-event-notification-templates).
- The timestamps in the email notifications are generated according to the time zone configured for the users who are selected to receive the notification. To learn more, see [About Users & Roles](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-users-roles#deception-add-new-user-admin-portal) and [Editing the User Profile](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/editing-user-profile).
- Deception enforces a Fair Usage Policy (FUP) that limits the number of notifications triggered per day. A [system message](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-logs-and-system-messages) is also generated when this limit is reached for the first time in a day. To learn more, see [Ranges & Limitations](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/ranges-and-limitations#orchestrate-limitations).

You can create a response rule to automatically contain users or devices. Deception integrates seamlessly with various security solutions to isolate active attackers and devices. You can create a rule to forward the attacker's identity to the integrated solution, which then isolates the attacker's system from the network. To learn more, see [About Containment Integration](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-containment-integration).

To create a response action, under the **Respond**section, configure a containment action:

1. Enable one or more integrations that you want to use to contain identities. See image.
2. Select additional options if you are configuring the following containment solutions:
  - **Palo Alto Networks - NGFW**: You can choose to contain attackers based on their hostnames or IP addresses per the External Dynamic List. See image.
  - **Fortinet**: You can choose to contain attackers based on their domains or IP addresses per the Threat Feeds. See image.
  - **CrowdStrike Falcon Insight**: You can contain endpoints based on the following parameters:
    - IOC Hash
    - IOC IP
    - IOA Process Tree
  - **Okta (SSF)**: Select **Enabled** and configure the user risk level and risk change reason that you want to be pushed to Okta: See image.
    - **User Risk Level**: Select a risk score level (**Low**, **Medium**, or **High**) that you want to be pushed to Okta for a user when an event matching the configured rule condition occurs. This information is shared with Okta.
    - **Risk Change Reason**: Enter the reason describing why the risk score is changed. This information is shared with Okta.

- **IOC Hash**: Enable to share file hashes that are considered indicators of compromise with CrowdStrike.
- **IOC Hash Action**: Choose the action that CrowdStrike should perform when IOC hashes are shared:
  - **Detect Only**: Show the indicator as a detection and take no other action.
  - **Block**: Add the indicator to the denylist and show it as a detection.
  - **Block, Hide Detection**: Add the indicator to the denylist and do not detect it.
  - **Allow**: Add the indicator to the allowlist and do not detect it.
  - **No Action**: Save the indicator for future use and take no action.
- **IOC Hash Severity**: Designate an appropriate severity level for indicators that should be shared with CrowdStrike. The available levels are **Informational**,**Low**, **Medium**,**High**,and **Critical**.

See image.

- **IOC IP:**Enable to share IP addresses that are considered indicators of compromise with CrowdStrike.
- **IOC IP Action**: Choose the action that CrowdStrike should perform when IP addresses are shared:
  - **Detect Only**: Show the indicator as a detection and take no other action.
  - **No Action**: Save the indicator for future use and take no action.
- **IOC IP Severity**: Designate an appropriate severity level for indicators that should be shared with CrowdStrike. The available levels are **Informational**,**Low**, **Medium**,**High**,and **Critical**.

See image.

- **IOA Process Tree**: Enable to share process trees that are considered indicators of attack with CrowdStrike.
- **IOA Action**: Choose the action that CrowdStrike should perform when IOA process trees are shared:
  - **Detect**: Show the indicator as a detection and take no other action.
  - **Monitor**: Use the indicator for informational use only and take no action nor show it as a detection.
  - **Block Execution**: Kill the process and show the indicator as a detection. Exercise caution when choosing the Block Execution action as CrowdStrike kills all processes that match with the process tree across all endpoints in your network. To avoid killing legitimate processes, make sure that you have configured IOA safe processes as described in the [Containment Configuration Guide for CrowdStrike](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/containment-configuration-guide-crowdstrike).
- **IOA severity**: Designate an appropriate severity level for indicators that should be shared with CrowdStrike. The available levels are **Informational**,**Low**,**Medium**,**High**,and **Critical**.

See image.

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-python-based-handler-cve-datasets","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540681"} -->
## Creating a Python-Based Handler for CVE Datasets

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-python-based-handler-cve-datasets
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Miragemaker > Application Datasets > Vulnerable Application Datasets > Creating a Python-Based Handler for CVE Datasets
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to create a Python-based handler for CVE datasets.

A CVE handler is a Python file that teaches a decoy how to respond to exploit attempts targeting a specific vulnerability. When an attacker sends a request matching a known CVE, the handler returns a convincing fake response, making the decoy appear vulnerable which lures the attacker in.

Each handler file lives at `datasets/aicve/<CVE-ID>.py` and is validated by an AST parser before it can be uploaded. This article covers every rule the validator enforces.

- Step 1: Creating the Python Handler
- Step 2: Validating the Python Handler

## File Structure

A handler file has three required pieces, all defined at the top level of the module:

- `CVE_ID`: A string constant identifying the vulnerability.
- One or more handler functions (async functions) that accept a [request](https://starlette.dev/requests/) and return a [response](https://starlette.dev/responses/).
- `ROUTES`: A list that maps HTTP methods and URL paths to your handler functions.

Beyond these pieces, you can add imports, constants, and helper functions as needed. The validator only inspects the required pieces.

### CVE ID

Assign `CVE_ID` as a plain string literal at the module level. It cannot be computed from a function call, read from a file, or defined inside a conditional block.

`CVE_ID = "CVE-2024-12345"`

### Handler Functions

Each handler function must meet the following conditions:

- Async: Declared with `async def`, not plain `def`.
- Single-parameter: Accepts exactly one argument (the Starlette `Request` object).
- Annotated with `-> Response` and the return type must be `Response`.

At runtime, you can return any Starlette response subclass (`PlainTextResponse`, `HTMLResponse`, etc.), but the annotation must say `Response`.

```
async def handle_info(request: Request) -> Response:
return Response(status_code=200, content="ok")
```

If a function is not referenced in `ROUTES`, the validator ignores it entirely. Only routed handlers are checked.

### ROUTES

`ROUTES` must be a list literal assigned at the module level. Each entry is a dict with three required keys:

- `METHOD`: A string literal. Must be `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`.
- `PATH`: A string literal starting with `/.` Supports Starlette path parameters like `{id}` or `{rest:path}`.
- `HANDLER`: A bare reference to one of your async handler functions (not a string or call, but just the function name).

```
ROUTES = [
{"METHOD": "POST", "PATH": "/api/login", "HANDLER": handle_login},
]
```

Duplicate routes (same method and path) within a single handler file are rejected.

#### Path Parameters

If the exploit targets a dynamic URL, use Starlette path parameter syntax in your `PATH` value. A `{name}` segment matches a single path component, while `{name:path}` matches everything including slashes. Inside your handler, access captured values through `request.path_params`.

```
plugin = request.path_params["plugin"]
rest = request.path_params.get("rest", "")
```

## Session Store

Many CVEs involve multistep exploit flows. For example, authenticating first to get a token, then using that token in a follow-up request. The session store lets you persist state across requests without any external dependencies.

Access it via `request.state.sessions`. It provides 4 async methods:

- `create(data={...}, ttl=300)`: Creates a new session and returns a UUID key.
- `get(key)`: Retrieves session data, or `None` if expired or missing.
- `set(key, data, ttl=300)`: Stores data under a specific key.
- `delete(key)`: Removes a session.

All data lives in memory and is lost on the decoy restart, which is by design for decoy interactions.

## Helpers and Imports

You can import any module from the Python standard library and define as many helper functions or constants as you need. The validator does not inspect helpers and imports. It only checks `CVE_ID`, `ROUTES`, and the functions referenced by `ROUTES`.

## Validation Error Reference

When the validator rejects a file, it returns a specific error message. Review the following error messages:

- `Syntax errors`: The file isn't valid Python. Fix the syntax issue reported at the given line number.
- `Handler must assign CVE_ID as a string`: Either `CVE_ID` is missing, or it's assigned to something other than a string literal (e.g., a function call or variable).
- `Handler must define ROUTES as a list literal`: Either `ROUTES` is missing, or it's assigned to something other than a `[...]` list expression.
- `ROUTES entry N: must be a dict`: The Nth element in the list isn't a `{...}`dict literal.
- `ROUTES entry N: missing required key "X"`: The dict is missing `METHOD`, `PATH`, or `HANDLER`.
- `ROUTES entry N: METHOD must be a string literal` or `ROUTES entry N: "X" is not a valid HTTP method`: The method is either not a plain string or not one of the 7 accepted methods.
- `ROUTES entry N: PATH must be a string literal` or `ROUTES entry N: PATH must start with /`: The path is either not a plain string or doesn't begin with a forward slash.
- `ROUTES entry N: duplicate route "GET /path"`: Another entry in the same file already uses this exact method and path combination.
- `ROUTES entry N: HANDLER must be a function reference, not a literal`: You passed a string like `"handle_info"` instead of the bare name `handle_info`.
- `ROUTES entry N: HANDLER "X" is not defined as an async function`: The referenced name either doesn't exist in the file or is a regular `def` instead of `async def`.
- `ROUTES entry N: handler "X" must accept exactly 1 parameter`: The function takes zero or more than one argument. It must accept exactly one.
- `ROUTES entry N: handler "X" must have return type annotation -> Response`: The function is missing a return type annotation, or the annotation is something other than `Response`.

To validate the Python handler:

1. Download the validator. [Download](https://help.zscaler.com/downloads/deception/miragemaker/application-datasets/vulnerable-application-datasets/creating-python-based-handler-cve-datasets/cve_validator.txt) The validator file is downloaded in TXT format.
2. Rename the file by changing the extension from `.txt` to `.py`.
3. Place both the handler you created and the validator you downloaded in the same directory.
4. Open the terminal and go to the folder where the handler and validator are located.
5. Run the validator using the following command: `python3 <validator-file-name>.py --file-path <handler-file-name>.py`If validation is successful, the following message is shown: `OK: <handler-file-name>.py`If validation is unsuccessful, the following message is shown: `FAIL: <error-message>`
6. If the validation is successful, you can [upload the dataset to the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/adding-vulnerable-application-dataset).
<!-- /ZS-ARTICLE -->

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-rds-decoy-aws","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540560"} -->
## Creating an RDS Decoy in AWS

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-rds-decoy-aws
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > AWS > Creating an RDS Decoy in AWS
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure an RDS decoy in AWS.

The Relational Database Service (RDS) in Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a web service that allows you to set up and host relational databases (MySQL or PostgreSQL) on the cloud. You can create RDS decoy databases (public or private) based on MySQL or PostgreSQL to lure adversaries that are looking for databases to disrupt services or steal data. Optionally, the credentials of the master user of the database along with the URL can be added to a [landmine policy](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-policies) as a lure.

Zscaler Deception uses Amazon RDS's db.t3.micro instance type to create RDS decoys. To learn more about Amazon RDS instance types, refer to the [AWS Documentation](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/instance-types/).

## Prerequisites

Before creating an RDS decoy in AWS, you must ensure that you have:

- Configured the [integration between AWS and Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-aws).
- (Optional) Obtained the necessary CloudShell command for the deployment script using one of the following methods: This only applies to the CloudShell-based deployment.
  - [Automated Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-direct-download-script-aws)
  - [Manual Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-manual-download-script-aws)

## Creating an RDS Decoy

To create an RDS decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **AWS**> **RDS**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **RDS Decoy** window appears.
3. In the **RDS Decoy** window: See image.
  - **Name**: Enter a name for the RDS database decoy.
  - **Account ID**: Select the Account ID associated with the AWS account in which you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Region**: Select the AWS region in which you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Description**: Enter a description relevant to the RDS database decoy.
  - **Engine Type**: Select a database type (**MySQL**or **PostgreSQL**) from the drop-down menu.
  - **Engine Version**: Select a supported version of the database engine from the drop-down menu.
  - **Publicly Accessible**: Enable if you want the decoy to be accessible to anyone. Otherwise, if it is disabled, access to the decoy is limited to internal adversaries.
  - **Subnet Group**: Enable to deploy the decoy in a subnet group belonging to an existing VPC, then enter the subnet group name.
  - **VPC CIDR**: Enter the address in CIDR format for the VPC where you want to deploy the decoy. If a VPC is not available, a new VPC is created. This option is available only if **Subnet Group**is disabled.
  - **Subnet CIDRs**: Enter the subnet IP address range in CIDR format for the VPC. This option is available only if **VPC CIDR** is configured.
4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoys based on the method used to configure the integration between AWS and Deception: If you want to add multiple RDS decoys to AWS, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then deploy all decoys simultaneously. Upon successful deployment, the RDS database decoy is added to AWS. The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the RDS decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > AWS > RDS) within the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. In addition, the **URI**value is automatically generated and associated with the public RDS decoys during the subsequent health check. The **URI**value is also shown in the RDS decoys table. To learn how to configure lures using RDS database decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using AWS Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-aws-decoys).
  - Terraform-based deployment
  - CloudShell-based deployment

1. On the **Cloud Deception - AWS** page, go to **Settings**.
2. Locate the AWS account you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
3. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
4. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `aws-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
5. Locate the `backend` block in the `aws-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of an S3 bucket-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "s3": { "bucket": "your-terraform-state-bucket", "key": "deception/terraform.tfstate", "region": "us-east-1", "encrypt": true } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same AWS account.
6. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
7. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
8. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted.
9. The necessary resources are deployed, and a JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
10. On the **Cloud Deception - AWS** page, go to **Settings**, locate the AWS account you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
11. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

1. Sign in to the [AWS Management Console](https://aws.amazon.com/console/) as an administrator.
2. Click the **CloudShell** icon on the navigation bar to launch AWS CloudShell. See image. The **AWS CloudShell**window appears.
3. In the **AWS CloudShell**window: See image.
  1. Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the [automated download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-direct-download-script-aws) or [manual download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-manual-download-script-aws).
  2. Enter the option to deploy RDS database decoys and press `Enter`. The deployment script detects the Account ID and deploys the RDS decoys to the selected regions.

## Creating an S3 Decoy in AWS

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-s3-decoy-aws
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > AWS > Creating an S3 Decoy in AWS
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure an S3 decoy in AWS.

The Simple Storage Service (S3) is an object-based storage service on Amazon Web Services (AWS). You can create AWS S3 decoys and associate [file datasets](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-file-datasets). Optionally, these S3 bucket URLs can be added to a [landmine policy](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-policies) to add lures to the endpoints. The S3 decoys can detect the following attack paths:

- Public: Adversaries can enumerate public S3 storage accounts by using keywords related to an organization to find exposed storage buckets on the internet in an attempt to steal sensitive data.
- Private: Adversaries with compromised identities of your organization can target storage buckets that are accessible via the compromised identities.

## Prerequisites

Before creating an S3 decoy in AWS, you must ensure that you have:

- Configured the [integration between AWS and Zscaler Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-aws).
- (Optional) Obtained the necessary CloudShell command for the deployment script using one of the following methods: This only applies to the CloudShell-based deployment.
  - [Automated Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-direct-download-script-aws)
  - [Manual Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-manual-download-script-aws)

## Creating an S3 Decoy

To create an S3 decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **AWS**> **S3**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **S3 Decoy**window appears.
3. In the **S3 Decoy** window: See image.
  - **Name**: Enter a name for the S3 decoy.
  - **Account ID**: Select the Account ID associated with the AWS account in which you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Region**: Select the AWS region in which you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **ACL**: Use the drop-down menu to choose your preferred access control list for the S3 decoy:
    - Select **Public**if you want the S3 decoy to be accessible to anyone.
    - Select **Private**if you want the S3 decoy to be accessible only to internal adversaries.
  - **Description**: Enter a description relevant to the S3 decoy.
  - **File Dataset**: Select a file dataset that you want to be hosted within the S3 bucket.
4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoys based on the method used to configure the integration between AWS and Deception: If you want to add multiple S3 decoys to AWS, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then deploy all decoys simultaneously. Upon successful deployment, the S3 decoy is added to AWS. The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the S3 decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > AWS > S3) within the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. To learn how to configure lures using S3 decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using AWS Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-aws-decoys).
  - Terraform-based deployment
  - CloudShell-based deployment

1. On the **Cloud Deception - AWS** page, go to **Settings**.
2. Locate the AWS account you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
3. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
4. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `aws-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
5. Locate the `backend` block in the `aws-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of an S3 bucket-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "s3": { "bucket": "your-terraform-state-bucket", "key": "deception/terraform.tfstate", "region": "us-east-1", "encrypt": true } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same AWS account.
6. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
7. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
8. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted.
9. The necessary resources are deployed, and a JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
10. On the **Cloud Deception - AWS**page, go to **Settings**, locate the AWS account you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
11. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

1. Sign in to the [AWS Management Console](https://aws.amazon.com/console/) as an administrator.
2. Click the **CloudShell** icon on the navigation bar to launch AWS CloudShell. See image. The **AWS CloudShell**window appears.
3. In the **AWS CloudShell**window: See image.
  1. Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the [automated download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-direct-download-script-aws) or [manual download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-aws#zd-manual-download-script-aws).
  2. Enter the option to deploy S3 decoys and press `Enter`. The deployment script detects the Account ID and deploys the S3 decoys to the selected regions.

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-secret-manager-decoy-gcp","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540675"} -->
## Creating a Secret Manager Decoy in GCP

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-secret-manager-decoy-gcp
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > GCP > Creating a Secret Manager Decoy in GCP
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to create a secret manager decoy in GCP.

A secret manager in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is a service used to securely store, manage, and control access to sensitive information such as API keys, passwords, certificates, and tokens. Secrets are stored centrally and accessed by applications through authenticated requests based on IAM permissions. You can create secret manager decoys containing fake secret identifiers or access references. Any attempt to access or enumerate these decoy secrets is detected and logged as an attack. You can view and analyze the attack details from the [Zscaler Deception dashboard](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/viewing-investigate-dashboard).

## Prerequisites

Before creating a secret manager decoy in GCP, ensure that you have configured the [integration between GCP and Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-gcp).

## Creating a Secret Manager Decoy

To create a secret manager decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **GCP**> **Secret Manager**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **GCP Secret Manager**drawer appears.
3. In the **GCP Secret Manager**drawer: See image.
  1. **Project**: Select the project in which you want to create the decoy.
  2. **Name**: Enter a name for the secret manager decoy.
  3. **Description**: Enter a description for the secret manager decoy.
4. Click **Save**. If you want to add multiple secret manager decoys to GCP, repeat the previous steps for each decoy and then deploy all decoys simultaneously.
5. On the **Cloud Deception - GCP**page, go to **Settings**.
6. Locate the GCP project you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
7. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
8. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `gcp-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
9. Locate the `backend` block in the `gcp-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of Google Cloud Storage bucket-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "gcs": { "bucket": "your-terraform-state-bucket", "prefix": "deception/terraform" } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same GCP project.
10. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and set the user agent for Terraform: `export TF_APPEND_USER_AGENT="<value_from_ui>"`
11. Run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
12. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
13. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted. The necessary resources are deployed.
14. Run the following command to export the state file as JSON: `terraform output -json gcp_terraform_output > deployment-output.json`The JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
15. On the **Cloud Deception - GCP** page, go to **Settings**, locate the GCP project you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
16. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. Upon successful deployment, the secret manager decoy is added to GCP. The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the secret manager decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > GCP > Secret Manager) within the Deception Admin Portal. To learn how to configure lures using secret manager decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using GCP Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-gcp-decoys).

[Image: Adding secret manager decoy in GCP]

[Image: Adding a secret manager decoy in GCP]

[Image: Downloading Terraform files for GCP]

[Image: Terraform deployment steps showing the option to download Terraform files]

[Image: Uploading Terraform files to the  Zscaler Deception Admin Portal]

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-service-account-decoy-gcp","lastmod":"2026-08-03T00:19Z","nid":"1540674"} -->
## Creating a Service Account Decoy in GCP

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-service-account-decoy-gcp
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > GCP > Creating a Service Account Decoy in GCP
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to create a service account decoy in GCP.

A service account in Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is a special type of account used by applications or services to authenticate and interact with Google Cloud resources. A service account is identified by its unique email address. You can create service account decoys with API credentials that can be placed in credential files on endpoints using landmine decoys. Any enumeration using these credentials is detected and logged as an attack. You can view and analyze the attack details from the [Zscaler Deception dashboard](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/viewing-investigate-dashboard).

## Prerequisites

Before creating a service account decoy in GCP, ensure that you have configured the [integration between GCP and Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-gcp).

## Creating a Service Account Decoy

To create a service account decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **GCP**> **Service Account**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **GCP Service Account**drawer appears.
3. In the **GCP Service Account**drawer: See image.
  1. **Project**: Select the project in which you want to create the decoy.
  2. **Name**: Enter a name for the service account decoy.
  3. **Description**: Enter a description for the service account decoy.
4. Click **Save**. If you want to add multiple service account decoys to GCP, repeat the previous steps for each decoy and then deploy all decoys simultaneously.
5. On the **Cloud Deception - GCP**page, go to **Settings**.
6. Locate the GCP project you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
7. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
8. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `gcp-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
9. Locate the `backend` block in the `gcp-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of Google Cloud Storage bucket-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "gcs": { "bucket": "your-terraform-state-bucket", "prefix": "deception/terraform" } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same GCP project.
10. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and set the user agent for Terraform: `export TF_APPEND_USER_AGENT="<value_from_ui>"`
11. Run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
12. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
13. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted. The necessary resources are deployed.
14. Run the following command to export the state file as JSON: `terraform output -json gcp_terraform_output > deployment-output.json`The JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
15. On the **Cloud Deception - GCP** page, go to **Settings**, locate the GCP project you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
16. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. Upon successful deployment, the service account decoy is added to GCP. The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the service account decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > GCP > Service Account) within the Deception Admin Portal. To learn how to configure lures using service account decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using GCP Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-aws-decoys).

## Creating a Service Principal Decoy in Azure

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-service-principal-decoy-azure
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > Azure > Creating a Service Principal Decoy in Azure
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure a service principal decoy in Microsoft Azure.

Service principals are identities created for use with applications, hosted services, and automated tools to access Microsoft Azure resources. You can create service principal decoys with credentials attached to them. Any attempt to sign in using the credentials of the service principals will be detected as an attack or compromise. These service principal decoys have access to all other Azure decoys that are part of the decoy resource group (Decoys Resource Group) [configured by Zscaler Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure). The most effective way to lure attackers using decoy users is to add these decoy users to a [landmine policy](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-policies).

## Prerequisites

Before creating a service principal decoy in Azure, you must ensure that you have:

- Configured the [integration between Microsoft Azure and Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure).
- (Optional) Obtained the necessary PowerShell command to run the deployment script using one of the following methods: This only applies to the Cloud Shell-based deployment.
  - [Automated Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script)
  - [Manual Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script)

## Creating a Service Principal Decoy

To create a service principal decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **Azure**> **Service Principal**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **Service Principal Decoy** window appears.
3. In the **Service Principal Decoy** window: See image.
  - **Name**: Enter a name for the service principal decoy.
  - **Tenant ID**: Select the tenant ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Subscription ID**: Select the subscription ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Description**: Enter a description relevant to the service principal decoy.
4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoy based on the method used to configure the integration between Azure and Deception: If you want to add multiple service principal decoys to Microsoft Azure, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then run the script to sync all decoys simultaneously.
  - Terraform-based deployment
  - Cloud Shell-based deployment
6. Enable Azure AD (Entra ID) diagnostic settings: This configuration is not handled via the deployment script, as enabling diagnostic settings via API requires a P1 or P2 subscription.
  1. In the Azure Portal, click **Azure Active Directory**. See image.
  2. Go to**Monitoring**> **Diagnostic settings**.
  3. Click **Add diagnostic setting**. See image. The **Diagnostic setting**window appears.
  4. In the **Diagnostic setting**window:
    1. Enter a **Diagnostic setting** name.
    2. Under the **Logs**section, select the **ServicePrincipalSignInLogs** checkbox to configure a data source for sending the logs to the logging storage account created as a part of the integration.
    3. Under the **Destination details**section, select the **Archive to storage account**checkbox,and select the storage account created as part of the integration from the **Storage account**drop-down menu. See image.
    4. Click **Save**.

Upon successful deployment, the service principal decoy is added to Microsoft Azure under the Decoys Resource Group configured by Deception [during the integration](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure). In addition, a **Client ID**is also associated with the service principal automatically. The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the service principal decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > Azure > Service Principal) within the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal.

To learn how to configure lures using service principal decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using Azure Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-azure-decoys).

1. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**.
2. Locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
3. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
4. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
5. Locate the `backend` block in the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of an Azure blob storage-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "azurerm": { "resource_group_name": "your-tfstate-rg", "storage_account_name": "yourtfstatestorageacct", "container_name": "tfstate", "key": "deception/terraform.tfstate" } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same Azure account.
6. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
7. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
8. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted. The necessary resources are deployed.
9. Run the following command to download the details of the state as a JSON file. `terraform output -json decoys_output > deployment-output.json`A JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
10. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**, locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
11. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

1. Sign in to the [Azure Portal](http://https://portal.azure.com) as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.
2. Launch Cloud Shell by clicking the **Cloud Shell** icon on the top navigation bar. See image. The **Cloud Shell** window appears.
3. In the **Cloud Shell** window: See image.
  1. Set your shell environment to PowerShell.
  2. Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the [automated download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script) or [manual download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script).
  3. Enter the option to deploy user decoys and press `Enter`.

## Creating a Storage Account Container Decoy in Azure

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-storage-account-container-decoy-azure
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > Azure > Creating a Storage Account Container Decoy in Azure
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure a storage account container decoy in Microsoft Azure.

A storage account container in Microsoft Azure is a type of cloud storage used for storing unstructured data. You can create storage account container decoys and associate [file datasets](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-file-datasets) with them. Optionally, these storage account container decoys can be added to a [landmine policy](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/about-policies) to add lures on the endpoints. The storage account container decoys can detect the following attack paths:

- Public: Adversaries can enumerate public storage accounts using keywords related to an organization to find exposed storage account containers on the internet in an attempt to steal sensitive data.
- Private: Adversaries with compromised identities of your organization can target storage account containers that are accessible via the compromised identities.

## Prerequisites

Before creating a storage account container decoy in Azure, you must ensure that you have:

- Configured the [integration between Microsoft Azure and Zscaler Deception](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure).
- (Optional) Obtained the necessary PowerShell command to run the deployment script using one of the following methods: This only applies to the Cloud Shell-based deployment.
  - [Automated Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script)
  - [Manual Download Method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script)

## Creating a Storage Account Container Decoy

To create a storage account container decoy:

1. Go to **Deceive**> **Cloud Deception**> **Azure**> **Storage Account Container**.
2. Click **Add Decoy**. See image. The **Storage Account Container Decoy** window appears.
3. In the **Storage Account Container Decoy** window: See image.
  - **Name**: Enter a name for the storage account container decoy.
  - **Tenant ID**: Select the tenant ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Subscription ID**: Select the subscription ID of the Azure account where you want to deploy the decoy.
  - **Resource Group**: If this is your first decoy in the account (Tenant ID and Subscription ID combination) or if you want to create a new resource group, enter a name for the resource group that must hold the decoy. If there is an existing resource group for the account (Tenant ID and Subscription ID combination), select the resource group from the drop-down menu.
  - **Region**: Select the region where the decoy must be deployed from the drop-down menu. If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.
  - **Storage Account**: Enter the name of the storage account to which you want to add the container.
  - **ACL**: Use the drop-down menu to select your preferred access control list for the container decoy:
    - **Container**: Allows anonymous access to the container and blobs.
    - **Blob**: Allows anonymous access only to the blobs.
    - **Private**: Doesn't allow anonymous access to the container and blobs.
  - **Description**: Enter a description relevant to the storage account container decoy.
  - **File Dataset**: Select a file dataset that you want to be hosted within the container.
4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoy based on the method used to configure the integration between Azure and Deception: If you want to add multiple storage account container decoys to Microsoft Azure, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then run the script to sync all decoys simultaneously.
  - Terraform-based deployment
  - Cloud Shell-based deployment

Upon successful deployment, the storage container decoy is added to Microsoft Azure. The storage container decoy is part of the Decoys Resource Group configured by Deception [during the integration](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/setting-cloud-deception-microsoft-azure). The deployment status is indicated by the icon next to the name of the decoy in the storage account container decoys table (Deceive > Cloud Deception > Azure > Storage Account Container) within the Zscaler Deception Admin Portal. To learn how to configure lures using storage container decoys, see [Configuring Lures Using Azure Decoys](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/configuring-lures-using-azure-decoys).

1. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**.
2. Locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Download**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
3. In the **Terraform Deployment Steps**window, click **Download**to download the necessary files. See image. A ZIP file containing all necessary files is downloaded to your system.
4. Extract the downloaded ZIP file and open the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file in a text editor.
5. Locate the `backend` block in the `azure-decoys.tf.json` file. Add your back-end details and save the file. The following example shows a `backend` block of an Azure blob storage-based Terraform back end: `{ "terraform": { "backend": { "azurerm": { "resource_group_name": "your-tfstate-rg", "storage_account_name": "yourtfstatestorageacct", "container_name": "tfstate", "key": "deception/terraform.tfstate" } } } }`Ensure that you use the same back end for all configurations relating to the same Azure account.
6. In the terminal, go to the extracted folder, and run the following command to create a new workspace: ``terraform init && terraform workspace new``<workspace_name>``
7. Run the following command to deploy resources: `terraform apply`
8. Review the plan, and confirm it by entering `Yes` when prompted. The necessary resources are deployed.
9. Run the following command to download the details of the state as a JSON file. `terraform output -json decoys_output > deployment-output.json`A JSON file containing the details of the state is downloaded.
10. On the **Cloud Deception - Azure**page, go to **Settings**, locate the Azure account you added, and click the **Upload**icon in the **Actions**column. See image.
11. Select the downloaded JSON file to update the status to the Deception Admin Portal.

1. Sign in to the [Azure Portal](http://https://portal.azure.com) as a Cloud Device Administrator or Global Administrator.
2. Launch Cloud Shell by clicking the **Cloud Shell** icon on the top navigation bar. See image. The **Cloud Shell** window appears.
3. In the **Cloud Shell** window: See image.
  1. Set your shell environment to PowerShell.
  2. Run the deployment script using the command obtained via the [automated download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-direct-download-script) or [manual download method](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/obtaining-deployment-script-azure#zd-manual-download-script).
  3. Enter the option to deploy user decoys and press `Enter`.

## Creating a Storage Account File Share Decoy in Azure

- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Deceive  > Cloud Deception > Azure > Creating a Storage Account File Share Decoy in Azure
- Last modified: 2026-08-03T00:19Z
- Summary: How to configure a storage account container decoy in Microsoft Azure.

A storage account file share in Microsoft Azure is a file share service mountable on endpoints and can be Server Message Block (SMB) protocol or Network File System (NFS) protocol. Zscaler Deception allows you to create storage account file share decoys that include decoy file datasets and mount them on endpoints to lure adversaries.

## Prerequisites

Before creating a storage account file share decoy in Azure, you must ensure that you have:

If there is an existing resource group for the account (Tenant ID and Subscription ID combination), select the resource group from the drop-down menu.

If you are creating a new resource group while adding the decoy, the resource group is created in the region selected for the decoy. However, when selecting an existing resource group, the deployment region of the decoy and the resource group can be different.

4. Click **Save**.
5. Deploy the decoy based on the method used to configure the integration between Azure and Deception: If you want to add multiple storage account file share decoys to Microsoft Azure, repeat Step 1 to Step 4 for each decoy and then run the script to sync all decoys simultaneously.

<!-- ZS-ARTICLE {"url":"/deception/creating-strategy","lastmod":"2025-05-21T20:20Z","nid":"1539315"} -->
## Creating a Strategy

- Source: https://help.zscaler.com/deception/creating-strategy
- Product: Deception
- Path: Deception Help > Miragemaker > Strategy Builder > Deception Strategy > Creating a Strategy
- Last modified: 2025-05-21T20:20Z
- Summary: How to create a strategy to quickly configure decoys and detect threats.

You can create a custom strategy to configure Network decoys, Threat Intelligence (TI) decoys, Active Directory (AD) decoys, and Landmine policies on a single page. When you create a strategy, you define a list of personalities or tags that must be deployed together to run a deception campaign for a particular use case. For example, when you configure a strategy for ransomware, you enable the endpoints ransomware detection feature along with network share decoys on the network.

## Prerequisites

Before you create a Deception strategy, identify the following requirements:

- A use case such as Log4j, Conti Ransomware, etc.
- A department such as Information Technology (IT), Banking, Legal, Finance, etc.
- The type of decoys that are critical for deployment. For example, Network decoys, AD decoys, etc.
- The total number of decoys to be deployed.

## Creating a Strategy

To create a strategy:

1. Go to **Miragemaker**>**Strategy Builder**>**Deception Strategy**.
2. Click **Add Strategies**.

See image.

1. In the **Strategy Detail** window:
  1. On the **General** tab: See image.
    - **Name**: Enter the name of the strategy.
    - **Description**: Enter the description of the strategy.
  2. On the **Network Decoys** tab, click **Add** to create a Network decoy: See image.
    - **Use Tag**: Enable to choose a tag for the Network decoy.
    - **Personality/Tag**: Select a tag or personality from the drop-down menu. If **Use Tag** is enabled, this drop-down menu lists tags, otherwise it lists personalities.
    - **Count**: Enter the number of Network decoys you want to create for the selected personality or tag.
  3. On the **Threat Intelligence** tab, click **Add** to create a Threat Intelligence (TI) decoy: See image.
    - **Use Tag**: Enable to choose a tag for the TI decoy.
    - **Personality/Tag**: Select a tag or personality from the drop-down menu. If **Use Tag** is enabled, this drop-down menu lists tags, otherwise it lists personalities.
    - **Count**: Enter the number of TI decoys you want to create for the selected personality or tag.
  4. On the **Active Directory** tab, click **Add** to create an Active Directory (AD) decoy: See image.
    - **Use Tag**: Enable to choose a tag for the AD decoy.
    - **Personality/Tag**: Select a tag or personality from the drop-down menu. If **Use Tag** is enabled, this drop-down menu lists tags, otherwise it lists personalities.
    - **Count**: Enter the number of AD decoys you want to create for the selected personality or tag.
  5. On the **Landmine** tab, select decoy personalities from the **Personalities** drop-down menu. See image.
2. Click **Validate**to ensure that the corresponding Network, AD, and TI decoys are available for the configured landmine lures.

See image.

1. After the strategy is validated, click **Save**.

The strategy is created.

See image.

After the strategy is created, you can [deploy it](https://help.zscaler.com/deception/deploying-deception-strategy-using-internal-network-decoy).

[Image: The Deception Strategy page with an annotation around the Add Strategies button]

[Image: The Strategy Details window with an annotation around the General tab]

[Image: The Strategy Details window with an annotation around the Threat Intelligence tab]

[Image: The Strategy Details window with an annotation around the Active Directory tab]

[Image: Landmine strategies validated on the Strategy Details window]

[Image: The Deception Strategy page with an annotation around the new strategy that is added]
